Two fluids

A heat exchanger has a stream of each of two fluids, and a sheet can hold the states of both. This page follows Help › Examples › Heat exchanger with two fluids.

States of two fluids

In the evaporator of a water chiller, R-134a enters at 3.2 bar with x = 0.2 and leaves at 10 °C. It cools 0.6 kg/s of water at 1 bar, which enters at 15 °C. This sheet finds the water's exit state and the heat transfer rate.

fluid r134a
p_r = 3.2 [bar]; p_w = 1 [bar]
m_dot_r = 0.12 [kg/s]; m_dot_w = 0.6 [kg/s]
state 1 : p = p_r, x = 0.2
state 2 : p = p_r, T = 10 [C]
state 3 (water) : p = p_w, T = 15 [C]
state 4 (water) : p = p_w, h = h_4
m_dot_r*(h_2 - h_1) = m_dot_w*(h_3 - h_4)
Q_dot = m_dot_w*(h_3 - h_4)
check T_3 > T_2
check T_4 > T_1

Dome gives h_4 = 30.315 kJ/kg, T_4 = 7.1714 °C and Q_dot = 19.699 kW. Both checks pass.

  1. The fluid line sets the fluid of every state line that names none, so states 1 and 2 are R-134a.
  2. A state of another fluid names it in parentheses after its label: state 3 (water) : ….
  3. state 4 (water) : p = p_w, h = h_4 gives state 4 an h the sheet has not found yet. The balance finds h_4, and Dome then fixes state 4 from p_w and h_4.
  4. The fluids share one set of labels, so each state needs a label of its own. A second state 1, of either fluid, is an error.
  5. The States tab has a Fluid column when the states are of more than one fluid. Here it shows R-134a for states 1 and 2 and water for states 3 and 4.
  6. A state line that names no fluid takes the sheet's. Without (water), state 3 is R-134a at 1 bar and 15 °C, a superheated vapor. Errors and warnings, below, shows the message and the States tab.
  7. The streams flow in opposite directions. The water entering (3) meets the refrigerant leaving (2), and the water leaving (4) meets the refrigerant entering (1).
  8. Heat flows from the warmer fluid to the colder one at each end, so both checks must pass. With m_dot_r = 0.2 [kg/s], T_4 = 1.9679 °C and the second check fails.

The example opens this sheet with comments and a T–s diagram of the refrigerant.

One balance across both fluids

The same exchanger, written with property functions in place of state lines. Use this form when a balance needs only each stream's h, and no states table or diagram. Each function names its fluid, so the sheet needs no fluid line.

p_r = 3.2 [bar]; p_w = 1 [bar]
m_dot_r = 0.12 [kg/s]; m_dot_w = 0.6 [kg/s]
h_1 = h(r134a, p = p_r, x = 0.2)
h_2 = h(r134a, p = p_r, T = 10 [C])
h_3 = h(water, p = p_w, T = 15 [C])
m_dot_r*(h_2 - h_1) = m_dot_w*(h_3 - h_4)
T_4 = T(water, p = p_w, h = h_4)

Dome gives the same h_4 = 30.315 kJ/kg and T_4 = 7.1714 °C.

  1. Each fluid's h counts from a reference of its own: R-134a from its tables' reference, water from the steam tables'.
  2. Write each stream's change as a difference of two values of one fluid, as in m_dot_w*(h_3 - h_4). Each reference then cancels.
  3. Each stream keeps its own mass flow rate.
  4. A plot line needs state lines. Added to this sheet, plot Ts : 1 -p- 2 draws no states, and the figure shows "no state 1, 2 in the sheet".
  5. The form m_dot_r*h_1 + m_dot_w*h_3 = m_dot_r*h_2 + m_dot_w*h_4 also works, since each fluid has a term on each side. It gives the same h_4.
  6. A difference of h between two fluids, such as h_3 - h_2, is an error. Errors and warnings, below, shows it.

One diagram per fluid

A figure shows the states of one fluid on that fluid's saturation dome. Two plot lines draw the two streams of the first sheet.

fluid r134a
p_r = 3.2 [bar]; p_w = 1 [bar]
m_dot_r = 0.12 [kg/s]; m_dot_w = 0.6 [kg/s]
state 1 : p = p_r, x = 0.2
state 2 : p = p_r, T = 10 [C]
state 3 (water) : p = p_w, T = 15 [C]
state 4 (water) : p = p_w, h = h_4
m_dot_r*(h_2 - h_1) = m_dot_w*(h_3 - h_4)
plot Ts : 1 -p- 2
plot Ts : 3 -p- 4

Dome draws two figures, the first of the R-134a and the second of the water, each on its own tab of the figure pane.

  1. Write one plot line for each fluid.
  2. A figure takes the fluid of its first state. With plot Ts : 1 -p- 2 -- 3 -p- 4, Dome draws the water states on the R-134a diagram. The figure then shows the note "state 3 is water; this figure is r134a".
  3. States and diagrams gives the diagrams and paths.

Errors and warnings

Each entry gives a sheet, the message Dome shows for it, and what to change.

An h of one fluid less an h of another

fluid r134a
p_r = 3.2 [bar]; p_w = 1 [bar]
state 2 : p = p_r, T = 10 [C]
state 3 (water) : p = p_w, T = 15 [C]
dh = h_3 - h_2

h_3 is measured from the steam tables' reference and h_2 from the R-134a tables' reference; use one reference for every stream.

The two values count from different zeros, or references, so their difference has no meaning. Write each stream's change from two states of its own fluid: m_dot_w*(h_3 - h_4) for the water.

A state without its fluid

fluid r134a
p_r = 3.2 [bar]; p_w = 1 [bar]
m_dot_r = 0.12 [kg/s]; m_dot_w = 0.6 [kg/s]
state 1 : p = p_r, x = 0.2
state 2 : p = p_r, T = 10 [C]
state 3 : p = p_w, T = 15 [C]
state 4 (water) : p = p_w, h = h_4
m_dot_r*(h_2 - h_1) = m_dot_w*(h_3 - h_4)

h_3 is measured from the R-134a tables' reference and h_4 from the steam tables' reference; use one reference for every stream.

State 3 names no fluid, so it takes the fluid line and is R-134a. The first columns of the States tab show it:

StateFluidPhasep [bar]T [°C]
1R-134atwo-phase3.22.4768
2R-134asuperheated3.210
3R-134asuperheated115
4watercompressed liquid155.636

Write state 3 (water) : p = p_w, T = 15 [C]. With (water) left off states 3 and 4 both, every state is R-134a and Dome gives no message, so read the phase of each state.

One label for two states

fluid r134a
state 1 : p = 3.2 [bar], x = 0.2
state 1 (water) : p = 1 [bar], T = 15 [C]

state 1 is defined twice

Give the water states labels of their own, such as 3 and 4.
